newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Foreigners flee S.African golds in bullion's wake.
newsitem.headline: Foreigners flee S.African golds in bullion's wake.

text.p: Gold's latest thumping at the hands of speculative investment funds cut a swathe through South African gold shares on Wednesday as foreigners baled out, fearful of a lengthy bear phase for the metal, analysts said.

"The lack of support for gold shares is really coming from overseas -- look at the volumes that are starting to come back from across the water," said Trevor Pearton, head of mining research at Societe Generale Frankel Pollak.
Analysts said gloom was likely to shroud gold stocks for some time, eroding any strength that might have been won from expected rich fourth quarter earnings due to be unveiled this month.

"The guys are getting trapped into the psychology that there is no hope for gold, and locally it's probably a bit of desperation selling. I don't think that it's likely we're going to see much growth in the valuation of our market while there is this negative sentiment around," Pearton said.

The price of gold was fixed in London at $352.45 an ounce on Wednesday morning, the lowest setting since October 4, 1993, dragging the Johannesburg Stock Exchange gold share index down around three percent.
Western Areas shed 275 cents to 60.50 rand, Driefontein was down 175 cents at 44 rand and Kloof dropped 125 cents to 60.50 rand.

Few South African gold mines were seen immediately threatened by gold's dive below $353 an ounce as they were still earning fair amounts in rand terms following the rand's 29 percent slide against the dollar in 1996.
But knocks would be dealt to gold shares by overseas investors, unwilling to hold gold counters while bullion falls.
South African mines begin their fourth quarter gold results reporting on Thursday, with Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd kicks off at about 1400 GMT.

Gold Fields is in the spotlight after its wretched third quarter. Analysts said last quarter that the mining house was staring into an abyss, but they said on Wednesday that Gold Fields could surprise with satisfactory December earnings.

"This time around, after some really bad quarters, Gold Fields are going to be looking somewhat better. We'll see better numbers from both Kloof and Driefontein. This might set the tone for some more support," Pearton said.
Nevertheless, Gold Fields and other mining houses would suffer from the weaker bullion this first quarter, other analysts added.
Instead of basking in expected strong earnings, mines would be called upon to assure investors that they could weather bullion's feebleness.

"What I am hoping to hear is that people are looking carefully at their productivity. In view of the current gold price, we are going to have to get more efficient," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.
Meanwhile, most local investors were likely to hold their current positions, awaiting further signs from the investment funds as to where they planned to take bullion.
"It's going to be a wait and see situation. The trend on the gold price at the moment is down. The speculative funds are running it," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.

"They have got the bit between their teeth and as long as the EMU (European Monetary Union) stutters and stammers about what it's going to do as far as gold holdings are concerned, the speculators are going to have a field day."
